about.title: Watsonville Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Watsonville draws steady foot traffic through its downtown corridor, grocery stores along Airport Boulevard, and businesses stretched along Green Valley Road. When a property owner lets a spill, broken pavement, or poor lighting go unaddressed, a routine errand can end in a hard fall. California law requires showing the property owner knew or reasonably should have known about the hazard and failed to fix it or warn visitors in time. That's why what happens in the minutes and days after a fall matters so much — photos of the hazard, any store surveillance footage, and the names of employees or witnesses can all shape a claim. LawProactive doesn't practice law or handle your case directly. Instead, we connect injured Watsonville residents with an independent attorney who can evaluate the hazard, the property owner's knowledge, and what evidence still exists before it disappears. There's no cost to get connected, and attorneys in our network work on contingency.

whyChoose.title: What Matters in a Watsonville Premises Case

items.title: Proving the Owner Had Notice
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard and failed to act. An attorney can help gather inspection records, complaint logs, or maintenance history to establish that notice.

items.title: Preserving Surveillance Footage Fast
items.desc: Many Watsonville stores and businesses overwrite security video within days or weeks. Acting quickly to request and preserve that footage can be critical to showing how the hazard formed and how long it existed.

items.title: Understanding Comparative Fault
items.desc: California is a pure comparative fault state, so even if you're found partly responsible for a fall, you may still recover a reduced amount. An attorney can help address any comparative fault arguments a property owner might raise.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Watsonville?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a claim against a private property owner. If a government-owned property was involved — for example, a public building or sidewalk maintained by the city — that deadline is much shorter and requires a formal claim first. It's best to get advice early so you don't miss a critical window.

items.question: What if I fell at a business near Main Street or Freedom Boulevard and didn't take photos?
items.answer: Photos help, but they're not the only evidence available. Store surveillance video, incident reports, and witness statements can often fill in gaps, especially in busier commercial areas. An independent attorney can help identify and request that evidence before it's lost.

items.question: Will my own carelessness ruin my claim?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California's pure comparative fault rule means you can still recover compensation even if you were partly at fault for the fall, though your recovery may be reduced by your percentage of fault. An attorney can help assess how much this might affect your specific situation.
